editor_spans.body: The Prime Minister's Motherwell speech rests on a single example: a community-run project on one Easterhouse estate. He praises it in his own words for being 'bottom-up', 'rooted in local values' and 'run by the local community and the people on the estate'. He then promises to take it 'nationwide', saying 'not a project on one estate, but the way we support everybody, everywhere'. The trouble is that these two things pull against each other. What made the Easterhouse project work was that nobody designed it centrally. Once it becomes national policy, run through DWP money, performance targets and audits, it starts to look like the 'top-down, tick box systems' he says he wants to replace. Projects that get scaled up tend to keep the name and lose what made them work. The real test of 'names not numbers' will be whether the new arrangements allow communities to run things that cannot be measured, and whether some of them are allowed to fail.

The warm language about care also contains a harder line on welfare. The speech says one in six young people are not in education, employment or training. It promises a country that will not 'get comfortable with the idea of kids in their 20s just being there on benefits'. And it ties the Scottish offer to Alan Milburn's review. Local employment support can be a more humane way of helping people into work. It can also be the delivery arm for stricter conditions on benefits. Calling the offer 'DWP devolution' does not say which one it will be. Holyrood should ask what rules on benefit conditions come with the powers before it treats them as a gift.

The speech's own evidence works against its main argument. It blames deindustrialisation on decisions 'taken hundreds of miles away', which presents the problem as one of distance rather than policy. Yet it also admits that after 27 years of a Scottish Parliament, Scotland is still deeply unequal. It cites a seven-year gap in men's life expectancy between Glasgow and East Renfrewshire, and empty shops at one in five in Dundee against one in twenty in Edinburgh. Bringing power closer clearly has not closed those gaps alone. Meanwhile the money actually named is small: £10 million, matched by the Scottish Government, for colleges, and £1 billion for research and innovation spread across the whole UK. As we noted when the No10 North offer was trailed, the Prime Minister is competing with Holyrood on devolution, its home ground. Saying Holyrood centralises too much is the easy part of that argument. The harder question the speech avoids is whether Scotland's regions will get extra money along with the new powers, or simply a share of what they already receive.

Story 5, from "Prime Minister makes offer to Holyrood to work together to empower Scottish regions", published 2026-10-15, from govuk-number-10; cited by 1 later Editor's Span
  · Because power was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament, the Prime Minister will argue the next stage of devolution should place more decision-making in the hands of Scotland’s regions and cities to drive reindustrialisation.
  S352 (mentioning Andy Burnham {Q269909}, Scottish Government {Q32521}, Government of the United Kingdom {Q6063}, Number 10 North {Q140382294}, Scotland Office {Q277020}, Scotland {Q22}): As part of that offer, ⟦Andy Burnham⟧ will call on the Scottish Government to work with the UK Government through No10 North and the Scotland Office to develop a new model of regional empowerment for Scotland, ensuring communities with their own strengths, identity and ambitions can seize new economic opportunities and unlock their potential.
  · During my first week in office, I told the First Minister that I wanted to work with ⟦Scotland’s First Minister⟧ to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland’s regions and cities.
  S353 (spoken by Prime Minister Andy Burnham, mentioning Number 10 North {Q140382294}): Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this.
  · This is me making an offer to the Scottish Government.

  S354 (the Editor's): Read together, three announcements from one week show a single political strategy: Great British Railways' headquarters going to Derby, the 'No10 North' offer to Holyrood, and the apprenticeship pledges. Each moves institutions and decisions away from London. The Scotland offer goes further. It turns Westminster's devolution argument against the Scottish Government, calling it 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe.' That gives the Prime Minister a way to compete with Holyrood on its own ground while appearing to offer cooperation.
  · The timing for the railway is worth noting. Building at Becketwell starts in early 2027 and is due to finish by spring 2029. That is close to the latest date for the next general election, so the building meant to embody public ownership may only just be ready before voters judge it. Until then, the claimed benefits depend on things a minister can announce, such as a fare freeze and extra seats, rather than an organisation that already exists. The headline 600 apprenticeships are also spread over four years and sit within a much bigger youth employment scheme.
